_authority: Owner, 2026-10-15 (L48, 2.25.0): 'my main task is to level up pedagogy - bloom taxonomy needs to be on higher level. thats why we have tablets ... before that we used google docs/google classroom tasks, now we have tablets, so we can use all of their functionality to lift bloom taxonomy/pedagogy level up'. The Bloom map: what level each ILO asks for, what level each task reaches, where a task sits below its ILO, and which tablet task type would lift it. Read by scripts/bloom_map.py (and through it make_architecture_page.py and content_script.py); the judgement a list cannot make is in bloom/GUIDE.md. The revised taxonomy (Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001). Every floor here is a SUGGESTION in 2.25.0 - shown, never blocking. What is lifted is the TASK, up to the level its outcome asks for - never the outcome: the job sets the level, a higher level is not a better outcome, and there is no target share of higher-level outcomes ('rules' B3 and B7, 2.140.0).

rules._what: The seven rules for using Bloom of the Instructor-Led Course Design Framework (Aigars Kluga, 2 Nov 2026) - with the TLA Pool and Modality Matrix, the rules behind the Instructor-Led Course Development Guideline (L68). Bloom is a tag on each outcome and a check that teaching and assessment match the tag. It does not choose the method: the task type does (instructor-led.json R2), because Bloom describes thinking and says nothing about what the hands must learn or how people behave towards each other. 'where' names what in the factory carries each rule. None of them blocks: the Bloom findings are suggestions.

B1.rule: Tag every outcome: one Bloom level per outcome in the outcome register.
B1.where: bloom_map.py reads the level of every Main ILO and Sub-ILO; one it cannot read is said (b_unknown), never guessed

B2.rule: Never raise a regulator's outcome by rewording it. If the job needs more than the approved wording, add a sub-outcome at the higher level beside it. In-house outcomes are ours: set the level the job needs.

B3.rule: The job sets the level. A higher level is not a better outcome. A must-know rule stays at Remember, however critical; it is stated plainly and drilled.
B3.where: bloom/GUIDE.md 5 ('Remember is a right answer'); pedagogy_review.py refuses a level above the outcome without the task on board that needs it

B4.rule: Check for tags that are too low - the common error. An outcome written as 'knows' or 'describes' whose real job task is a decision belongs at Evaluate, and gets a sub-outcome that says so.
B4.where: instructor_led.py check, under C5 for the reviewer: a Sub-ILO read at or below 'at_or_below' whose task type is one of 'task_types', or that has a must-pass criterion, is asked about - never a no

B5.rule: Align outcome, practice and assessment. The trainee practises at the tagged level at least once, and the assessment item sits at that level. An Evaluate outcome taught by lecture and tested by a recall question is misaligned.
B5.where: bloom_map.py module map: a question below its Sub-ILO (b_q_below), a Sub-ILO no module-check question reaches (b_sub_unchecked, floors.module_check_reaches_ilo), a Sub-ILO no practice reaches (b_sub_unpractised, floors.practice_reaches_ilo); content_script.py i_not_practised (L73)

B6.rule: Teach lower levels as prerequisites, not as separate lessons. A trainee cannot judge a permit without knowing the limits; that does not mean walking every topic up all six levels.
B6.where: bloom/GUIDE.md 3 and 5: a lift never removes the recall, and a topic is lifted toward its outcome's level only

B7.rule: Set no quota. There is no target share of higher-level outcomes; the mix follows the job tasks in the course.
B7.where: no floor in this file counts outcomes; floors.apply_plus_min_share counts QUESTIONS and is a suggestion

verb_guide._what: The Bloom Verb Guide for Course Developers (Aigars Kluga, 23 Nov 2026), the companion to the Instructor-Led Course Design Framework: how the verb of an outcome WE write is chosen - a Sub-ILO added beside a regulator's outcome, or an in-house outcome. Choose the verb last: fix the job task and the Bloom level first, then take the plainest verb at that level that an assessor can see or score. The verbs to use, when, and what to assess with are on each level below ('levels': use_when, write, example, assess_with). On the Bloom card nothing here blocks (2.141.0): bloom_map.py shows a note at the Stage 2 page where the operator approves the Sub-ILOs. In an instructor-led course the guideline check already refused a Sub-ILO whose verb cannot be watched (know, understand - C2); it now reads the guide's own list of such verbs ('avoid', "observable": false).
steps: Name the job task: what the person does on board with this knowledge, in one line.
Set the Bloom level from that task. Recalling a limit is Remember; deciding whether to allow entry is Evaluate.
Pick a verb from that level's row ('levels' 'write'), the plainest that fits. If none fits, the level is probably wrong: go back a step before reaching for another row.
Finish the sentence: verb + object + condition + standard. 'Decides whether to allow entry, given a completed permit and gas readings, in line with the company procedure.'
Test it: could two assessors watch or mark this and agree? Does the assessment item ask for the same verb? If not, change the verb or the item.

V1.rule: Regulator wording is never changed. The guide applies to in-house outcomes and to sub-outcomes added beside an STCW, GWO or OPITO outcome.
V1.where: L2; instructor-led.json R1; the notes below are for Sub-ILOs only, a Main ILO is never asked to change

V2.rule: One verb per outcome. 'List and explain' is two outcomes, or one outcome tagged at the higher level.
V2.where: bloom_map.py ilo_level: the highest verb that leads a clause is the level

V3.rule: Plain verb over impressive verb: English is a second language for most trainees and many instructors. 'Explain', not 'elucidate'.

V4.rule: Change the verb and as few other words as possible. When an outcome is raised or fixed, the topic and the scope stay as they were.
V4.where: a re-expressed Sub-ILO (ilo_map.py, status re-expressed with its why); bloom/GUIDE.md 2 and 5

depends._how: Verbs that change level with the task. The CONDITION in the outcome fixes which level it is, so it is always written: 'from a given list', 'with the SDS in hand', 'in an unfamiliar scenario'. 'how' is the question that tells the two apart. identify, explain, describe and calculate are in 'verbs' at the level the factory reads when nothing more is said; select, check and prepare are left out of 'verbs', so a Sub-ILO that opens with one is shown this question (b_depends) and its level is written on it ("bloom": 3). The first six rows are the guide's table; 'prepare' is the factory's row for the one verb of the guide's level table that programmes also use at another level.

identify.low_use: identifies a hazard symbol on a label
identify.high_use: identifies the hazard in an unfamiliar scenario
identify.how: Was the answer taught as a fact, or must it be worked out?

explain.low_use: explains why a tank is tested before entry
explain.high_use: explains why this reading rose in a case not seen before
explain.how: Is the reason repeated, or reasoned from new data?

describe.high_use: describes it in their own words with an example
describe.how: Would the taught wording alone earn the mark?

select.high_use: selects between two acceptable options and justifies the choice
select.how: Does a rule give the answer, or is there a trade-off?

check.low_use: checks a harness against the inspection list
check.high_use: checks a permit and decides whether it is adequate
check.how: Is it ticking items, or judging whether the whole is safe?

calculate.low_use: calculates with a given formula and given data
calculate.high_use: works out which data and method the problem needs

prepare.low_use: prepares the tank for entry by the procedure
prepare.high_use: prepares a toolbox talk or a plan of their own
prepare.how: Is something made ready by a procedure, or is a new plan or document produced?

avoid._how: Verbs no assessor can see happen, or that hide the real verb. Ask 'what would the trainee do to show this?' and write that. A Sub-ILO that OPENS with one gets a note on the Bloom card (b_verb_avoid) - the longest entry wins, 'be' also reads 'is' and 'are'. "observable": false - no assessor can see it happen, so in an instructor-led course it fails the guideline's own item C2 ('every sub-outcome has an observable verb', R1) exactly as know and understand already did: instructor_led.py check says no until the Sub-ILO is re-expressed, or justified in one line. The first two rows are also 'weak' below, which has its own note. The hard words can be watched - they are only hard to read - and the 'replace' rows are verbs with a level that are still better replaced than tagged: notes only.

rows.problem: happens inside the head and cannot be observed
rows.instead: state, explain, use or decide, depending on the job task

rows.problem: has no level and no evidence
rows.instead: the action the awareness should lead to: reports, refuses, checks

rows.problem: sounds observable but names no action
names a classroom activity; nobody can fail it
describes the session, not the trainee
rows.instead: what the trainee can do after the session

rows.problem: describes the process, not the result

rows.instead: explain, find out, judge, combine, write

replace.instead: what the assessor sees: dons, launches, completes

replace.problem: is confused with the instructor's assessment

actions._how: Bloom covers thinking only: it has no verbs for motor skills or for how people act towards each other. For these outcomes, name the action the assessor watches and add the standard - time, sequence, tolerance or must-pass step. Record a Bloom tag only for the thinking part of such an outcome (the go or no-go decision inside a drill, written on the Sub-ILO as "bloom": n); do not force a level onto the physical or behavioural part. The verbs are read from instructor-led.json 'formats' 'verbs' of the same task type (test_bloom_map pins that every verb here is there). A Sub-ILO that opens with one and has no level is told so (b_action) instead of 'its level could not be read'.

drill.outcome: a fixed sequence done with the hands
drill.example: Dons breathing apparatus and completes the pre-entry checks in the correct sequence within the set time

simulator.example: Orders helm and engine movements in time to hold the planned approach track

human_factors.outcome: what people say and do to each other
human_factors.example: Challenges an unsafe order from a senior officer using the agreed wording

before_after._how: The guide's rewrites: the job task sets the level, then the verb changes and the topic stays. The fourth stays at Remember on purpose - a must-know item is stated and drilled, not pushed up a level for its own sake (rule B3).

rows.weak: Understands the hazards of enclosed space entry
rows.problem: no visible action; the job task is a decision
rows.rewritten: Decides whether to allow entry from a completed permit and gas readings, with reasons

rows.weak: Is familiar with the safety data sheet
rows.rewritten: Uses a safety data sheet to select the PPE for a named cargo

rows.weak: Knows the MARPOL Annex I discharge rules
rows.problem: 'knows' hides whether recall or use is meant
rows.rewritten: Uses the Annex I discharge conditions to say whether a given discharge is permitted

rows.problem: unobservable, but recall is the right level here
rows.rewritten: States the general emergency alarm signal and the actions to take

rows.weak: Demonstrates knowledge of portable fire extinguishers
rows.rewritten: Extinguishes a small fire using the correct extinguisher for its class
rows.level: Drill; Apply for the choice of extinguisher

rows.weak: Discusses the importance of teamwork on the bridge
rows.rewritten: Challenges a navigation error made by a senior officer during a simulator scenario

_levels: use_when, write, example and assess_with are the Bloom Verb Guide's table (verb_guide, 2.141.0): 'write' is the short list of verbs to use when WE write an outcome at this level - each names something an assessor can see or mark; 'verbs' below is the wider list the level of ANY outcome is read with. 'examples' (three languages) is what a note offers when a weak verb is to be replaced.

means.en: recall a fact, a limit, a signal or a step with no aid

1.use_when: Recalling a fact, limit, signal or step with no aid
1.example: States the actions to take on hearing the general emergency alarm
1.assess_with: Short recall item or oral question

means.en: give the reason or the meaning in their own words

2.use_when: Giving the reason or the meaning in their own words
2.example: Explains why a tank is ventilated and tested before entry

means.en: do it - use a rule, a procedure or an aid in a routine case
means.lv: izdarīt - darbināt, iestatīt, izmērīt, veikt procedūru
means.ru: сделать - управлять, установить, измерить, выполнить процедуру

3.use_when: Using a rule, procedure or aid in a routine case
3.example: Uses an SDS to select the PPE for a named cargo
3.assess_with: Worked task with the aid in hand

means.en: find what matters or what is wrong in a situation - the cause, the fault, the hazard
means.lv: atrast cēloni, kļūmi, bīstamību reālā situācijā
means.ru: найти причину, неисправность, опасность в реальной ситуации

examples.en: compare, distinguish, diagnose, find the cause of

4.use_when: Finding what matters or what is wrong in a situation
4.example: Finds the cause of a rising gas reading from the readings and the tank history
4.assess_with: Scenario item with data to interpret

means.en: judge against criteria and commit to a decision, with the reason
means.lv: izlemt, ko darīt, un pamatot; izvērtēt kāda lēmumu
means.ru: решить, что делать, и обосновать; оценить чужое решение

5.use_when: Judging against criteria and committing to a decision
5.example: Decides whether to allow or refuse entry from a completed permit, with reasons
5.assess_with: Scenario decision with justification, oral probe

means.en: produce a new plan or document of their own

6.use_when: Producing a new plan or document
6.example: Drafts a toolbox talk for a non-routine job on their own vessel

verbs._how: How the level of an ILO is read. en: whole words, the script adds -s, -es, -ed, -ing (identify -> identifies, identified). lv and ru: word STEMS - anything that starts with the stem matches (aprakst -> apraksta, aprakstīt). Multi-word entries are phrases. An entry ending in $ is a whole word only (lv 'veic$' - so that 'veicināt', to promote, is not read as 'veikt', to carry out). The ILO's level is the HIGHEST of the verbs that lead a clause - the first verb, and any verb straight after a comma, a semicolon or a lead word (and, or, to; un, spēj; и, уметь) - so a noun deep in the object is not read as a verb. 'weak' verbs cannot be observed or measured: they get a level, and a note. A verb in more than one level in real use (select, determine, check, определить) is left OUT on purpose - the report says 'not in the list' and Claude judges it (bloom/GUIDE.md 2); for select and check the Bloom Verb Guide's own test is shown (verb_guide 'depends'). A starting list: add the verbs your programmes use. 2.141.0, the Bloom Verb Guide's table: every verb of 'levels' 'write' is read at its own level - compare moved from Understand to Analyse (in all three languages), and give an example of, read, sort, find the cause of, accept and refuse were added. 'prepare' was at Apply and is now left out of the English list like select and check: the guide writes it at Create (preparing a plan or a document), programmes also use it for making equipment ready by a procedure - so it is asked, never guessed (verb_guide 'depends'). 2.142.0, the ILO elevation spec's verb list (ilo-elevation.json 'write_verbs'): interpret moved from Understand to Analyse (in all three languages), and predict, relate and verify were added - so every verb a raised outcome may start with is read at its own level.

weak._why: These say what happens inside a head - nobody can watch a trainee 'know'. A programme's Main ILO keeps them (verbatim, L2); a Sub-ILO is re-expressed with a verb that can be watched, the operator approving (status re-expressed). STCW's own column 'knowledge, understanding and proficiency' is written this way - the level is still read from it.

lead_words._why: A verb straight after one of these leads a clause: 'and describe', 'to operate', 'spēj aprakstīt', 'уметь применять'.

mechanics._how: The level a tablet task type USUALLY reaches (typical), and the highest it CAN reach when it is written for it (ceiling) - with how. A question may state its own level ('bloom': 4, 'bloom_why': '...') when it is written above the usual; it is then shown as stated, and a stated level above the ceiling is pointed out. Create (6) is reached only by 'build the plan', written for it (2.28.0) - and in a narrow sense: the trainee composes a plan from given cards. Real creation stays with the practical exercise.

single_choice.higher: give a short real situation, and make the right option one that has to be worked out from it - not a fact recalled

multi_select.higher: a situation with several clues; the trainee picks every clue that points to the fault

cloze.higher: gaps that carry the reasoning (because ... so ...) rather than the facts

match.higher: match each situation to the action it needs, not a term to its definition

categorise.higher: sort observed symptoms into the causes behind them

order.higher: order the steps of a procedure the trainee will actually carry out, with the situation given

hotspot.higher: tap where you would act - the valve to close, the point to measure - not just where a part is

label_diagram.higher: label what each part does, not only its name

read_instrument.higher: read it, then say what the reading means for the operation

scenario.higher: at each step the trainee chooses the action AND the reason, and sees the consequence of a wrong one

build_the_plan.higher: give the situation the plan must fit, and cards from more than one procedure, so the trainee composes the plan for it

fill_matrix.higher: a situation that changes who does what - the trainee fills the whole grid for it, not a standard one recalled

timeline.higher: ask where it should have been stopped, and why - the feedback names the barrier that failed

true_false.higher: Part A - statements that state a reason ("... because ..."), not a bare fact

calculate.higher: give more data than is needed, so the trainee has to choose what applies

investigate.higher: add a source that rules out the tempting wrong conclusion, so the trainee has to weigh the evidence

take_apart.higher: ask what a part does from where it sits, then operate it

test_atmosphere.higher: follow it with the entry decision as its own question

dress_for_job.higher: the buddy check judges a colleague's choice - ask why one fault matters most

lay_out.higher: change the wind and ask what has to move

floors._apply_plus: A suggestion, not a rule (2.25.0): at least half of a module's self-check and module-check questions at Apply or higher. On paper and in Google Classroom almost everything was Remember; the tablet can let the trainee operate, find and decide. It counts QUESTIONS, never outcomes - there is no target share of higher-level outcomes (rule B7); the framework's own review line for written items is 'recall items are a minority'. A module whose outcomes are must-know facts may sit below it: Remember is a right answer (rule B3).
floors._reaches: A suggestion, not a rule (2.25.0): for every Sub-ILO the module check has at least one question at the Sub-ILO's level or higher - otherwise the module never checks what it promised.
floors._practice: A suggestion, not a rule (2.140.0, rule B5): for every Sub-ILO the module has at least one practice moment at the Sub-ILO's level or higher before it is checked - a self-check question, or an activity screen or active slide whose format's TLA carries that Bloom tag (instructor-led.json tla_pool). Compared up to Evaluate, as the module check is. Not counted when the module has no practice moment at all, or names no Sub-ILO on any of them.
